name: Eye yoga / eye exercises

card.summary: Eye movement and relaxation routines claimed to firm the eye area; no studies support an appearance effect.
card.note: Related Bates-method practices such as sungazing carry documented risks.

quick.overview:
Eye yoga is a set of eye-movement and relaxation routines. Some in looksmaxxing circles say it firms or brightens the eye area.

No studies were found testing this. Reviews of eye exercises for vision itself found no clear benefit.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners move or rest the eyes through set routines, on the theory that this relieves strain or tone in the surrounding muscles.
quick.risks: Plain eye movements are low-risk, but related Bates-method practices like sungazing or pressing on the eyes have documented risks, and abandoning glasses can be unsafe.

lead: Eye yoga, or eye exercises, is a set of routines of deliberate eye movements, palming, focus shifting and relaxation. In looksmaxxing circles, practitioners use it with the aim of relaxing the muscles around the eyes, reducing the strained, squinting or tired look that screen work can produce, and firming or brightening the eye area. The practice draws on a lineage that includes the Bates method, an alternative therapy developed by the American eye doctor William Horatio Bates (1860-1931).[1]

Proponents describe a chain in which relaxed eyes and less strain lead to a more open, rested expression and a fresher-looking periorbital area. No published study has tested eye exercises for the appearance of the skin or tissues around the eyes; research on eye exercises concerns vision, eye-movement disorders and sports performance.[2][3][2]

Reviews of vision training for eyesight itself, including a 2004 American Academy of Ophthalmology review and a 2005 review of 43 studies, report no clear improvement in visual acuity.[1] Orthoptic eye exercises are, however, an established part of clinical care for some eye-movement disorders such as convergence problems and double vision after neurological injury.[4][5]

angle.text: Practitioners use eye yoga to reduce strain around the eyes, with the aim of looking more rested and having a firmer, brighter eye area. Routines are typically done for a few minutes during or after screen use.

infobox: Palming, shifting and swinging the gaze, focus changes, eye rolling
Firmer, brighter, more rested eye area

paras: Techniques associated with the Bates method include palming (covering closed eyes with the palms without pressure), visualising small black letters or dots, and shifting or swinging the gaze.[1] Modern eye yoga routines commonly combine these with eye rolling, near-and-far focusing and blinking exercises, and are often promoted for people who spend long periods at screens.

Related clinical and sports routines exist under other names. Orthoptic exercises such as pencil push-ups and the Brock string are used in vision therapy, and athletes use focus-flip and ball-on-a-string drills to practise visual skills.[2][4]

The looks rationale offered by practitioners is that tension and fatigue around the eyes show as squinting, tired-looking lids and a drawn eye area, and that relaxing and exercising the eyes counters this. The idea parallels facial-exercise routines for other areas of the face.
No published trial has measured under-eye puffiness, lid position, wrinkles or skin firmness after eye exercises, so these effects are described by practitioners rather than documented in studies.

Bates reported in 1891 that he had reversed several cases of myopia, and in 1920 he self-published Perfect Sight Without Glasses.[1] In 1917 he partnered with Bernarr Macfadden on a correspondence course that the American Medical Association criticised, and in 1929 the US Federal Trade Commission filed a complaint over misleading advertising.[1] Aldous Huxley popularised the approach in The Art of Seeing (1942).[1] Chinese school eye exercises, a different tradition involving acupoint massage, have been taught to schoolchildren since the 1960s and are among interventions recommended in China's myopia-prevention plan.[3]

Laboratory measurements published in 1998 found that the eyeball changes length only minutely during focusing, far less than the Bates theory required.[1] The American Academy of Ophthalmology review found no objective evidence that visual training improves eyesight and attributed reported gains to factors such as better interpretation of blurred images, mood or the pinhole effect of the pupil.[1]

A 2023 systematic review of interventions recommended in China for children's myopia found that time outdoors and reduced near work lowered new myopia, and that all interventions had a limited effect on progression; eye exercises were among those assessed.[3]

Commentators on the Bates method note that sungazing can injure the eye, pressing on the eyeballs while palming may raise glaucoma risk, and abandoning corrective lenses can be unsafe or delay treatment of conditions such as glaucoma or amblyopia.[1] Gentle movements and palming without pressure are not associated with reported harms.
No studies found for eye exercises as a means of changing the appearance of the eye area.

Related research covers other uses. Reviews describe eye muscle exercises as part of treatment for eye-movement disorders and diplopia after neurological damage,[4][5] and a 2023 review assessed Chinese eye exercises among myopia-prevention measures with limited effects on progression.[3] Vision training for visual acuity has not shown clear benefit.[1]
